parsed.why: Police are documented as systematic perpetrators, using criminalisation for harassment and extortion; forced examinations and birth-sex-default detention add severe state exposure. Limited prosecutions do not mitigate documented police practice.

Ordinary visitor interactions are usually low-hostility, and courts have delivered meaningful protections. Bathhouse access and foreign-document handling pose uncertainties, while individual custody cases show serious resident exposure but no general visitor-facing policy.

Recent killings, documented violence, official warnings about impunity, and uneven enforcement make protections unreliable. Raw counts cannot establish prevalence, but the pattern and weak recourse outweigh positive legal frameworks and accepting urban venues.

Criminalising statutes remain but are reported unenforced; no trans-specific targeting or visitor-facing restrictions are documented. Thin evidence and discrimination without legal recourse lower confidence, while the statutes are a secondary—not decisive—risk.

Criminalisation is linked to arrests of LGBTQ people, concealment, and attackers exploiting identity; a harsher bill was actively proposed in 2024. Employment protection is resident-facing and cannot offset this exposure.
